pos: n. and v. (toil, work, the exertion of body or mind; rendering Hebrew amal and yagia, Greek kopos)
etymology: From the Latin labor, toil, hardship, distress, through Old French labour. The English keeps the Latin double sense of exertion and of the burden the exertion carries; a woman in travail is said to labour, and so is a ship straining in a heavy sea.
biblical_def: Labour is exertion at a task, and Scripture places it in the week before it places it under the curse. The fourth commandment assumes it as a creation ordinance: “Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work” (Exodus 20:9) — the command to rest on the seventh presupposes a command to work on the other six, and both are grounded in what God himself did in creating and resting. Adam dressed and kept the garden before he ever sinned; what the fall added was not labour but sweat, thorns, and frustration. Scripture therefore never treats work as the curse, and never treats idleness as the recovery of Eden. What it does insist on is that labour without God is empty motion: “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it” (Psalm 127:1). The vanity is not in the building but in the except. Our Lord draws the same line between two objects of labour: “Labour not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life” (John 6:27) — not a prohibition of daily work but a ranking of ends. And Paul closes the resurrection chapter by attaching the doctrine to the workbench: “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 15:58). Because the body will be raised, what the body does now is not swallowed up. The resurrection is the reason a Christian may work hard at small things.
webster_summary: Exertion of body or mind; toil; work. Scripture makes it a creation ordinance under the fourth commandment, pronounces it vain apart from the LORD, and by the resurrection declares it not in vain in the Lord.
webster_full: LABOR, LABOUR, n. [L. labor.] Exertion of muscular strength, or bodily powers, particularly when painful or accompanied with fatigue; toil.
2. Intellectual exertion; application of the mind to study or thought.
3. That which requires wearisome exertion; work performed.
4. Travail; the pangs and efforts of childbirth.
5. LABOR, v.i. To exert muscular strength; to act or move with painful effort, particularly in servile occupations; to work; to toil.
corruption_summary: Labour is turned into identity — a man's work made the answer to what he is — or else despised as the mere curse a wiser age would escape. Scripture gives it a lower place than identity and a higher place than curse.
corruption_paragraphs: The first misuse makes work the self. A calling becomes the whole answer to the question who a man is, so that unemployment is not a hardship but an unmaking, and retirement is a small death. The Bible will not carry that weight. A man is what he is before God in Adam or in Christ; his labour is what his hands are given to do in the station God set him in. The second misuse runs the other way and reads Genesis 3 as though work itself were the sentence passed on sin. It was not. The sentence was thorns, sweat, and the frustration of the ground — the same task made bitter, not a new task imposed. Read rightly, the curse is on the conditions of labour, and the redemption of labour is not its abolition but its restoration to fruitfulness.

The principle to recover is the one Paul puts at the end of the greatest chapter on the resurrection, where the argument descends without warning from the trumpet and the incorruptible body to steadiness at an ordinary bench: therefore be stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord (1 Corinthians 15:58). The doctrine of the empty tomb is the reason a nursing mother, a farmer, and a clerk may pour out years on work no one will remember. Nothing done in the Lord falls to the ground, because the Lord who receives it was raised, and what he receives he keeps.
roots_summary: Hebrew amal is toilsome labour, often with the sense of the trouble it costs; yagia is the produce that labour wins. Greek kopos is wearying work, and ergon the work done.
roots_lines: Hebrew amal (H5999) — toil, trouble, wearisome labour; the word Ecclesiastes uses for all the labour under the sun.
Hebrew yagia (H3018) — the fruit or earnings of toil; thou shalt eat the labour of thine hands.
Hebrew abad (H5647) — to work, to serve, to till; used of Adam in the garden before the fall.
Greek kopos (G2873) — wearying toil, labour to the point of fatigue; your labour of love.
Greek ergon (G2041) — work, deed, the thing accomplished; the work of the Lord in 1 Corinthians 15:58.
usage: Of the creation ordinance: six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work (Exodus 20:9).
Of labour's emptiness apart from God: except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it (Psalm 127:1).
Of the ranking of ends: labour not for the meat which perisheth (John 6:27).

pos: n. (a fitting or appointed time; a division of the year; rendering Hebrew eth and moed, Greek kairos)
etymology: Through Old French seson from the Latin satio, a sowing — the year divided by when the seed goes in. The agricultural root is exactly right for the biblical idea: a season is not a stretch of time but the right time for a particular thing.
biblical_def: A season in Scripture is less a quarter of the year than a fitting moment appointed by God. Ecclesiastes states the doctrine at the head of its most quoted chapter: “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven” (Ecclesiastes 3:1). The point is not that all times are equal but that each thing has its own, and the man who plants at harvest or mourns at a wedding has misread not his calendar but his providence. The blessed man of the first Psalm is fruitful precisely on this schedule: he “bringeth forth his fruit in his season” (Psalm 1:3) — not perpetually, not on demand, but when the appointed month comes round. Paul makes the seasonal principle a rule for reaping: “in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Galatians 6:9), where the whole weight rests on due; the harvest is certain and the date is not ours. Yet the same apostle sets one duty deliberately outside the rule, charging Timothy to preach the word and “be instant in season, out of season” (2 Timothy 4:2). Everything else waits for its hour; the preaching of the word does not. That single exception tells us what the Lord counts urgent.
webster_summary: A fitting or convenient time; a division of the year. Scripture makes it the appointed hour for a particular thing — fruit in his season, reaping in due season — and exempts only the preaching of the word.
webster_full: SEASON, n. se'zn. [Fr. saison; L. satio, a sowing.] A fit or suitable time; the convenient time; the usual or appointed time.
2. A time of some continuance, but not long; as a season of fair weather.
3. One of the four divisions of the year, spring, summer, autumn, winter.
4. SEASON, v.t. To render palatable, or to give a higher relish to, by the addition of some article.
5. To fit for any use by time or habit; to mature; to prepare.
corruption_summary: The season is abolished by a culture that expects everything to be available at once, and Ecclesiastes 3 is quoted as a call to serene acceptance rather than as a doctrine of God's appointment.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors converge on this word. The first is practical: strawberries in January and an answer to every question in an instant have trained a generation to regard waiting as a defect in the system rather than a fixture of the world God made. Where nothing has a season, patience has no soil to grow in, and the man who has never waited for anything has no category for a promise that ripens slowly. The second error is in how Ecclesiastes 3:1 is preached. Detached from the God who does the appointing, it becomes a piece of mild fatalism — everything comes round in time, so be at peace. But Solomon's conclusion is not serenity; it is fear of God (Ecclesiastes 3:14). The seasons are not a wheel turning of itself. They are the ordered acts of a sovereign who set the times and the bounds of our habitation.

The principle to recover is that the appointed hour belongs to God and the faithfulness belongs to us. Galatians 6:9 divides the labour from the timing with great care: in due season we shall reap, if we faint not. Our part is the not fainting; his part is the due season. Much discouragement in the Christian life comes from taking up his half of that verse and setting our own date for the harvest — and then, when the date passes, concluding that the sowing was wasted.
roots_summary: Hebrew eth is time in the sense of the right occasion; moed is an appointed meeting or set feast. Greek kairos is the opportune moment, as distinct from chronos, duration.
roots_lines: Hebrew eth (H6256) — time, the fit occasion; the word repeated through Ecclesiastes 3.
Hebrew moed (H4150) — an appointed time, a set feast, a meeting fixed beforehand.
Hebrew zeman (H2165) — a stated or appointed season, chiefly in the later books.
Greek kairos (G2540) — the opportune, decisive moment; the word behind in due season.
Greek chronos (G5550) — duration, elapsed time; the measured stretch, not the fitting hour.
usage: Of the appointment of times: to every thing there is a season (Ecclesiastes 3:1).
Of fruitfulness on God's schedule: he bringeth forth his fruit in his season (Psalm 1:3).
Of the one duty outside the rule: be instant in season, out of season (2 Timothy 4:2).

pos: n. and v. (travel from one place to another; a day's march; rendering Hebrew derek and massa, Greek hodoiporia)
etymology: From Old French journee, a day's work or a day's travel, from Latin diurnus, of a day. The buried word is day: a journey was originally as far as a man could go between one sunrise and the next, which is why the KJV can speak of a three days' journey or a sabbath day's journey.
biblical_def: A journey is travel with a destination, and Scripture uses it both plainly and as the shape of the believing life. Abraham's servant, sent to find a wife for Isaac, is watched by a man who “held his peace, to wit whether the LORD had made his journey prosperous or not” (Genesis 24:21) — the journey is the ordinary business of travel, but its prospering is referred without embarrassment to the LORD. Our Lord in his humiliation is found “wearied with his journey” (John 4:6), sitting on Jacob's well at the sixth hour; the incarnation is real enough to produce tired feet, and it is a tired Christ who offers living water. The prodigal “took his journey into a far country” (Luke 15:13), and the phrase carries the whole doctrine of departure: a journey away from the father's house is still a journey, purposeful, funded, and chosen. Luke measures the return from Olivet as “a sabbath day's journey” (Acts 1:12) — a short, exact distance, the rabbinic limit for travel on the seventh day. The Scriptures thus keep the word firmly literal. What later Christian speech makes of it — the pilgrim traveling toward the city that hath foundations — is a legitimate extension, but it is built on real roads and real weariness, not on metaphor alone.
webster_summary: Travel from one place to another; properly, a day's travel. Scripture keeps it literal — a prospered errand, a wearied Christ at a well, a far country chosen — and lets the pilgrim sense rest on that solid ground.
webster_full: JOURNEY, n. jur'ny. [Fr. journee, from jour, a day; L. diurnus.] The travel of a day.
2. Travel by land to any distance and for any time, indefinitely; as a journey from London to Paris.
3. Passage from one place to another; as a long journey.
4. JOURNEY, v.i. To travel; to pass from place to place.
5. In Scripture, the removals of the Israelites in the wilderness are called their journeys.
corruption_summary: The word has been drained of destination. Journey now names a process valued for itself — it is the journey, not the arriving, that matters — which is precisely the opposite of the biblical use.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern religious speech has made journey a favourite because it can be used to postpone every question of arrival. A man is on a journey of faith, on a journey of discovery, and the word quietly grants him permission never to conclude anything. Where a destination is not named, no course can be wrong, no doctrine can be settled, and repentance has nothing to turn toward. Scripture never speaks this way. Every journey in the Bible has a terminus that can be reached or missed: the servant's errand prospers or it does not; the prodigal arrives in the far country and later arrives home; the disciples walk a measured distance back to Jerusalem. Even the great pilgrim passages fix the end — a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God (Hebrews 11:10).

The principle to recover is that Christian travel is toward something. Bunyan understood the word better than the modern usage does: his pilgrim has a Celestial City in view from the first page, and every by-path is measured against it. To speak of the Christian life as a journey is faithful only when the destination is named and the road is one that can be left. Take away the destination and the word becomes a way of walking nowhere in particular and calling it growth.
roots_summary: Hebrew derek is a way, road, or the course of travel upon it; massa is the pulling up of stakes, a setting forward by stages. Greek hodoiporia is wayfaring, from hodos, a way.
roots_lines: Hebrew derek (H1870) — way, road, journey; also the moral course a man walks.
Hebrew massa (H4550) — a breaking up of camp, a setting forward; the stages of the wilderness marches.
Hebrew halak (H1980) — to go, to walk, to journey; the common verb of travel and of conduct.
Greek hodoiporia (G3597) — a wayfaring, a journey; the word of John 4:6.
Greek hodos (G3598) — a way, road; also the name the first Christians bore, this way.
usage: Of an errand referred to God: whether the LORD had made his journey prosperous or not (Genesis 24:21).
Of the Lord's true weariness: Jesus therefore, being wearied with his journey, sat thus on the well (John 4:6).
Of deliberate departure: took his journey into a far country (Luke 15:13).

And the man wondering at her held his peace, to wit whether the LORD had made his journey prosperous or not.

Luke 15:13

pos: n. and adv. (one's own dwelling; the place of belonging; rendering Hebrew bayith, Greek oikos and idios)
etymology: From the Saxon ham, a dwelling, village, or estate — surviving in English place-names ending in -ham. Unlike house, which names the structure, home has always named the belonging: the house one returns to.
biblical_def: Home in the Authorized Version is where a man belongs and returns, and Scripture gives it three uses worth distinguishing. First, it is a place of witness. The delivered Gadarene begged to follow Christ, and was refused with an errand instead: “Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee” (Mark 5:19). The first mission field is the house one came from, and the first congregation is the people who knew the man before. Second, it is a place of duty, and the Lord himself provides one from the cross: “And from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home” (John 19:27). Dying for the sins of the world, he does not overlook the housing of his mother. Paul reasons the same way when he charges widows' children to shew piety at home before anywhere else (1 Timothy 5:4); religion that has not yet reached the household is not ready to be exported. Third, and most soberly, home is used of the grave and of heaven. Ecclesiastes says of the aged that “man goeth to his long home” (Ecclesiastes 12:5), and Paul balances the two dwellings: “whilst we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:6). That verse quietly unsettles every earthly hearth. The believer's present address is a temporary one, and the homesickness he cannot explain is accurate.
webster_summary: One's own dwelling and place of belonging. Scripture makes it the first mission field, the first field of duty, and — against every earthly hearth — the place the believer is not yet at.
webster_full: HOME, n. [Sax. ham, a house, a village.] A dwelling house; the house or place in which one resides.
2. One's own country; as, to return home from a foreign land.
3. The place of constant residence; the seat of family or of domestic life.
4. HOME, adv. To one's habitation or country; as, go home; return home.
5. Closely; to the point; as, to press an argument home; the reproof came home to him.
corruption_summary: Home is reduced to a private refuge from the world — a place to be comfortable rather than a place to be faithful — while the believer's real homelessness in this world is quietly forgotten.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern house is sold as a sanctuary from obligation: a place where a man is finally off duty. Scripture reverses this. Home is where duty is densest, because it is where the people are whom God has actually given us to serve. Timothy is told that piety is proved at home before it is displayed anywhere else (1 Timothy 5:4); the Lord in his dying hour secures a roof for his mother (John 19:27); and the healed man of Gadara is sent home precisely because the hardest audience for a testimony is the household that remembers the man in his chains. A Christianity that is impressive in public and slack at its own table has failed the first examination.

The principle to recover is Paul's uncomfortable arithmetic: whilst we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:6). Both halves are true at once. The Christian is genuinely at home here — God gave him this body, this house, these people, and gratitude is the right response — and he is genuinely away from home, because the Lord he loves is elsewhere. Ecclesiastes calls the grave a man's long home to make the same point from the other side. Comfort here is real; permanence here is not.
roots_summary: Hebrew bayith serves for both house and household, structure and family together. Greek oikos is the house and those in it; idios, one's own, gives the sense of home in several passages.
roots_lines: Hebrew bayith (H1004) — house, household, family; the structure and the people are one word.
Hebrew ohel (H168) — tent, dwelling; the patriarchs' home, portable by design.
Greek oikos (G3624) — house, household; the root of oikonomia, stewardship of a house.
Greek idios (G2398) — one's own; rendered home where the sense is one's own place.
Greek endemeo (G1736) — to be at home, to be among one's own people; the verb of 2 Corinthians 5:6.
usage: Of the first mission field: go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee (Mark 5:19).
Of duty provided from the cross: that disciple took her unto his own home (John 19:27).
Of the believer's divided address: whilst we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:6).
scriptures: Mark 5:19
Howbeit Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him, Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee.
John 19:27
Then saith he to the disciple, Behold thy mother! And from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home.
Ecclesiastes 12:5

Also when they shall be afraid of that which is high, and fears shall be in the way, and the almond tree shall flourish, and the grasshopper shall be a burden, and desire shall fail: because man goeth to his long home, and the mourners go about the streets:
2 Corinthians 5:6
Therefore we are always confident, knowing that, whilst we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord:

pos: n. (a running, a set path or race; an appointed order of service; rendering Hebrew machaloqeth, Greek dromos and trochos)
etymology: From the Latin cursus, a running, from curro, to run, through Old French cours. The athletic image is original and is exactly what Paul intends: not a direction merely, but a track laid out and run to its end.
biblical_def: Course in the Authorized Version is a track run to its finish. Paul uses it twice of his own life, and both times the emphasis falls on completion rather than distance: “so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus” (Acts 20:24), and at the end, “I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7). A course is not chosen by the runner; it is received, as the ministry in Acts 20 is received. The believer's business is to finish what was assigned, not to design something more impressive. The word is also used of the free running of the gospel itself: Paul asks prayer “that the word of the Lord may have free course, and be glorified” (2 Thessalonians 3:1) — the word is pictured as a runner whose track men may obstruct or clear. James turns the image to terrible account, saying of the tongue that it “setteth on fire the course of nature” (James 3:6): the whole wheel of a man's life, running from birth to death, catches from that small flame. Behind these lies the Old Testament use for the twenty-four priestly courses, the appointed rotations of temple service — Zacharias was ministering in the order of his course when Gabriel came.
webster_summary: A running; the track run and the order appointed. Paul receives his course rather than choosing it and measures success by finishing; the word of the Lord runs a course men may clear or block.
webster_full: COURSE, n. [Fr. cours; L. cursus, from curro, to run.] In its general sense, a passing; a moving, or motion forward.
2. The ground, path or line in which motion is made; as the course of a river.
3. Order of succession; turn; as the courses of the priests in the temple service.
4. Line of conduct; manner of proceeding; as, he took a prudent course.
5. A methodical series, as a course of lectures; also, regular succession, as in the course of nature.
corruption_summary: The course is treated as self-chosen — a life one designs and may redesign — where Scripture presents it as received from the Lord, with faithfulness measured by finishing rather than by choosing well.
corruption_paragraphs: The governing modern assumption is that a life is a blank track on which a man lays out his own route, and that the mark of a life well lived is having chosen an interesting one. Paul's language cuts across this at the root. He speaks of “the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus” (Acts 20:24) in the same breath as his course, because the two are the same thing: the assignment and the track are given together. He does not congratulate himself on having selected an unusual life; he reports that he finished the one handed to him. This is why 2 Timothy 4:7 can be an old man's comfort. He is not claiming that his course was the greatest; he is claiming it is done.

The principle to recover is that faithfulness is measured against the assignment, not against other runners. A course is a fixed length; a man who runs three quarters of a long one has not outdone the man who finished a short one. The priestly courses make this concrete — Zacharias's week of service was not less holy for being one of twenty-four rotations. Most Christian discouragement dissolves once the runner grasps that the track was measured out for him by someone else, and that the only question at the end is whether he finished it.
roots_summary: Hebrew machaloqeth is a division or rotation, used of the priestly courses. Greek dromos is a race-course or the running of it; trochos is a wheel, the round of life in James 3:6.
roots_lines: Hebrew machaloqeth (H4256) — a division, a course of priests or Levites in their appointed rotation.
Hebrew derek (H1870) — way, course of life; the moral track a man runs.
Greek dromos (G1408) — a race-course, a running; Paul's word for the course he finished.
Greek trochos (G5164) — a wheel, a round; the course of nature set on fire in James 3:6.
Greek trecho (G5143) — to run; used of the word of the Lord having free course, 2 Thessalonians 3:1.
usage: Of a life assigned and completed: I have finished my course, I have kept the faith (2 Timothy 4:7).
Of the gospel running unhindered: that the word of the Lord may have free course, and be glorified (2 Thessalonians 3:1).
Of the whole round of life set alight: setteth on fire the course of nature (James 3:6).

Acts 20:24

But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God.
2 Thessalonians 3:1
Finally, brethren, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may have free course, and be glorified, even as it is with you:
James 3:6

pos: n. and v. (speed, urgency; hurried and often unadvised movement; rendering Hebrew chippazon and mahar, Greek spoude)
etymology: From Old French haste, of Germanic origin, akin to the Saxon haest, violence or vehemence. The old sense carried more heat than mere speed — haste was hurry with agitation in it, which is why the KJV can set it against faith.
biblical_def: Scripture divides haste exactly, and the division is worth learning. There is a commanded haste, and there is a condemned one. At the first passover Israel ate “with your loins girded, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and ye shall eat it in haste” (Exodus 12:11) — redemption is an errand to be obeyed at once, and the posture of the meal preached the urgency of the deliverance. But haste born of unbelief is another thing. David confesses, “I said in my haste, I am cut off from before thine eyes” (Psalm 31:22), and the verse is an honest record of a conclusion reached too fast under pressure; the next clause overturns it, nevertheless thou heardest. Proverbs makes it a moral matter: “he that hasteth with his feet sinneth” (Proverbs 19:2), the feet outrunning the knowledge the previous clause says the soul lacks. And Isaiah puts the definitive word beside the cornerstone: “he that believeth shall not make haste” (Isaiah 28:16). That is not a commendation of sloth. It means that the man whose foundation is a tried stone laid by God has no need of panic; he can wait, because his security does not depend on his own speed. Faith produces a certain unhurriedness that unbelief can never counterfeit.
webster_summary: Speed, urgency, hurry. Scripture commands it at the passover and condemns it in the anxious heart, setting Isaiah's rule over both: he that believeth shall not make haste.
webster_full: HASTE, n. [Fr. hate; Sax. haest, violence.] Celerity of motion; speed; swiftness; dispatch; expedition.
2. Sudden excitement of passion; vehemence; precipitance.
3. The state of being urged or pressed by business; as, to be in haste.
4. HASTE, v.t. To press; to drive or urge forward; to push on.
5. HASTE, v.i. To move with celerity; to be rapid in motion.
corruption_summary: Speed is treated as a virtue in itself and slowness as failure, so that hurry is never examined for what usually drives it — unbelief that God will act unless we act first.
corruption_paragraphs: An age that measures everything by how quickly it arrives has no way to hear Isaiah 28:16. To be told that believing men do not make haste sounds like a rebuke of diligence, and it is not; Scripture commands promptness in obedience often enough, and the passover was eaten standing. What Isaiah rebukes is the hurry that comes from having no foundation. The context is a people making desperate arrangements — a covenant with death, a refuge of lies — because they will not trust the stone God is laying in Zion. Panic is what unbelief looks like when it is busy. The remedy is not a slower schedule but a surer foundation.

The principle to recover is that haste is a symptom to be read rather than a pace to be praised or blamed on its own. David's I said in my haste (Psalm 31:22) is the most useful phrase in the Psalter for this, because it lets a believer put a date on a false conclusion without disowning himself. Under pressure he concluded he was cut off; the conclusion was wrong; God heard him anyway. Every Christian has said something in his haste. Wisdom is not pretending otherwise, but learning to hold such verdicts loosely until the pulse has slowed.
roots_summary: Hebrew chippazon is hurried flight, the word of the passover; mahar is to hasten or be rash. Greek spoude is diligence or speed, and speudo, to hasten.
roots_lines: Hebrew chippazon (H2649) — hurried flight, trepidation; used of eating the passover in haste.
Hebrew mahar (H4116) — to hasten, to be rash or precipitate; often carrying blame.
Hebrew chush (H2363) — to hurry, to make speed; used both of eager obedience and of panic.
Greek spoude (G4710) — haste, earnestness, diligence; Mary went into the hill country with haste.
Greek speudo (G4692) — to hasten, to urge on; the shepherds came with haste to Bethlehem.
usage: Of commanded urgency in redemption: ye shall eat it in haste: it is the LORD'S passover (Exodus 12:11).
Of a false conclusion reached under pressure: I said in my haste, I am cut off from before thine eyes (Psalm 31:22).
Of the unhurriedness faith produces: he that believeth shall not make haste (Isaiah 28:16).
scriptures: Exodus 12:11

Psalm 31:22

Isaiah 28:16

pos: n. (the first point of a thing; origin, first cause; rendering Hebrew reshith, Greek arche)
etymology: From the Saxon beginnan, to begin. The Hebrew reshith is from rosh, the head — the beginning is the head of a thing, its chief and first part, which is why the same word can mean firstfruits.
biblical_def: Beginning is the Bible's first word and one of its largest doctrines. “In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 1:1) establishes that the universe had a starting point and that God did not — he is already there when the beginning begins, and the sentence refuses in six words every eternal-matter and self-generating-cosmos account men have devised. John deliberately reaches for the same phrase to say something further: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). Genesis says what happened at the beginning; John says who already was. The Word does not begin at the beginning; he is there, distinct from God (with God) and identical in nature (was God), which is the Trinitarian grammar of the whole New Testament in a single verse. The word is also used morally: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 9:10) — not the elementary stage a student later leaves behind, but the head and first principle from which all real wisdom proceeds. And Christ takes the term as a title: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” (Revelation 21:6). He is not merely present at both ends of history; he is what those ends are.
webster_summary: The first point or origin of a thing. Genesis dates the creation and leaves God undated; John finds the Word already there; Proverbs makes the fear of the LORD the head of wisdom; Christ takes the word as his own name.
webster_full: BEGINNING, n. The first cause; origin; as, God is the beginning of all things.
2. That which is first; the first state; commencement; entrance into being.
3. The rudiments, first ground or materials; as, the beginnings of an art.
4. The first part of a thing, as distinguished from the middle and the end.
5. In Scripture, used of the eternal Word, who was in the beginning with God, John 1.
corruption_summary: Genesis 1:1 is reduced to ancient poetry about origins rather than a statement of fact, and John 1:1 is read as though the Word merely began with God rather than being God.
corruption_paragraphs: Two attacks land on this word. The first treats Genesis 1:1 as myth or as theological poetry with no claim about what actually occurred — a move that leaves the verse religiously edifying and factually empty. But the Bible everywhere treats the creation as an event: our Lord grounds the law of marriage in what was done at the beginning (Matthew 19:4-6), and Paul grounds the order of the sexes in the order of the making. Empty the beginning of fact and those arguments collapse with it. The second attack is on John 1:1, where the Arian and the modern Jehovah's Witness reading makes the Word a first creature who began when the beginning did. John forecloses this by saying was rather than came to be, and by placing the Word with God and as God in the same breath. What began in verse 1 is not the Word; it is the world he made in verse 3.

The principle to recover is that beginnings are not merely early, they are governing. Reshith is from the word for head, and a head rules what follows. That is exactly the force of Proverbs 9:10: the fear of the LORD is not a beginner's stage in wisdom that a mature man graduates from, but the head under which all genuine wisdom stands. Learning that does not begin there does not arrive there later.
roots_summary: Hebrew reshith is the first, chief, or head part — beginning and firstfruits together. Greek arche is beginning, origin, and also rule or dominion, the two senses inseparable.
roots_lines: Hebrew reshith (H7225) — beginning, chief part, firstfruits; from rosh, the head.
Hebrew techillah (H8462) — commencement, the first time a thing is done.
Greek arche (G746) — beginning, origin; also rule, principality — what is first also governs.
Greek protos (G4413) — first, foremost in time or rank; Christ the first and the last.
Greek ginomai (G1096) — to come into being; the verb John pointedly does not use of the Word.
usage: Of the creation of all things: in the beginning God created the heaven and the earth (Genesis 1:1).
Of the eternal Word already there: in the beginning was the Word (John 1:1).
Of the head of all wisdom: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10).
scriptures: Genesis 1:1
In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
John 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
Proverbs 9:10
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.
Revelation 21:6
And he said unto me, It is done. I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end. I will give unto him that is athirst of the fountain of the water of life freely.

pos: n. (place; the room or position of another; rendering Hebrew tachath, Greek huper and anti in the substitutionary sense)
etymology: From the Saxon stede, a place or station, cognate with the German Statt and with English steady, homestead, instead. The root idea is a standing-place; to act in another's stead is to stand where he stood.
biblical_def: Stead is one of the most doctrinally loaded small words in the Authorized Version, because it is the ordinary English for substitution. On Moriah, “Abraham went and took the ram, and offered him up for a burnt offering in the stead of his son” (Genesis 22:13). The ram does not assist Isaac or set him an example; it takes his place on the wood, and Isaac walks down the mountain alive because something died where he would have died. That is the shape of the atonement in narrative form, three chapters before the word lamb has any theology attached to it. Genesis uses the same construction at the other end of a grief: God “hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel, whom Cain slew” (Genesis 4:25) — Seth stands in the room Abel left. Job uses it to demand real sympathy: “if your soul were in my soul's stead, I could heap up words against you” (Job 16:4), which is an exact statement of how cheap counsel is from a man who is not standing where the sufferer stands. And Paul uses it of the preacher's office: “we pray you in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20). The ambassador does not speak for himself; he occupies his master's place and speaks his master's words.
webster_summary: Place; the room or position of another. It is the Authorized Version's plain word for substitution — the ram in the stead of Isaac, the ambassador in Christ's stead — and it carries the atonement in a single syllable.
webster_full: STEAD, n. sted. [Sax. stede, a place; G. statt.] Place; the room which another had or might have.
2. In composition, a farm or dwelling place; as homestead, farmstead.
3. To stand in stead, to be of use or great advantage.
4. INSTEAD, adv. In the place or room of; as, put this instead of that.
5. In Scripture, of one offered or standing in the room of another; as the ram offered in the stead of Isaac, Gen. 22.
corruption_summary: Substitution itself is under attack. Penal substitutionary atonement is charged with being unjust or worse, and stead is quietly emptied so that Christ becomes an example or a victim rather than a substitute.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern objection to penal substitution is that it is arbitrary at best and monstrous at worst — punishing an innocent for the guilty is called a moral scandal, and the doctrine is set aside in favour of theories in which the cross chiefly demonstrates love, exposes violence, or defeats hostile powers. Each of those contains something true and none of them is the centre. Scripture's own picture is the ram in the thicket: Isaac is bound, the knife is raised, and God provides a life to be taken in the stead of the life that was forfeit. The substitution is not an unwilling third party seized at random; it is the Son given by the Father and giving himself, one Person in two natures, competent to stand in the room of many because of who he is. The objection collapses once the substitute is recognized as God himself in our nature rather than a bystander.

The principle to recover is that the ambassadorial sense in 2 Corinthians 5:20 depends entirely on the sacrificial sense in Genesis 22:13. A preacher stands in Christ's stead in the pulpit only because Christ stood in the sinner's stead at the cross. Strip out the substitutionary atonement and the phrase in Christ's stead becomes a mere formality of office. Keep it, and every faithful sermon is a man occupying a place he did not earn, begging men to be reconciled by a death he did not die.
roots_summary: Hebrew tachath means under, in the place of — the preposition of substitution. Greek anti is in exchange for; huper is on behalf of, and in sacrificial contexts, in the place of.
roots_lines: Hebrew tachath (H8478) — underneath, in the place of; the ram offered in the stead of Isaac.
Hebrew kopher (H3724) — a ransom, the price paid in another's room; from kaphar, to cover, atone.
Greek anti (G473) — over against, in exchange for; his life a ransom anti many.
Greek huper (G5228) — on behalf of, in the place of; Christ died huper the ungodly.
Greek presbeuo (G4243) — to be an ambassador; the office of standing in another's stead.
usage: Of the substitutionary sacrifice: offered him up for a burnt offering in the stead of his son (Genesis 22:13).
Of a place filled after loss: hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel (Genesis 4:25).
Of the preacher's office: we pray you in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:20).
scriptures: Genesis 22:13

And Abraham lifted up his eyes, and looked, and behold behind him a ram caught in a thicket by his horns: and Abraham went and took the ram, and offered him up for a burnt offering in the stead of his son.
Genesis 4:25

Job 16:4

pos: n. and v. (careful attention, watchful regard; rendering Hebrew shamar, Greek blepo and prosecho)
etymology: From the Saxon hedan, to observe, to guard, to care for. The old sense is custodial rather than merely mental — to take heed of a thing is to keep watch over it, which is why the Hebrew behind it is often shamar, the verb used of keeping a garden and keeping a commandment.
biblical_def: To take heed is to keep watch, and the Bible directs it at four objects in particular. First, at one's own way, with the word as the standard: “Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? by taking heed thereto according to thy word” (Psalm 119:9). Note the two halves — heed alone is mere carefulness; heed according to thy word is sanctification, because it measures the way against something outside the self. Second, at the danger of self-confidence: “let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12). The warning is aimed precisely at the man who feels no need of it, which is why it is placed after the wilderness examples; those who fell in the desert had all seen the sea divided. Third, at the truth already heard, lest it drift: “we ought to give the more earnest heed to the things which we have heard, lest at any time we should let them slip” (Hebrews 2:1). The image is nautical — a vessel carried past the harbour by an unnoticed current. Apostasy is rarely a decision; it is usually a drift. Fourth, at the minister's own soul and message together: “Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine” (1 Timothy 4:16). Paul will not let the two be separated, and the order is significant.
webster_summary: Careful attention; watchful regard. Scripture points it at one's way measured by the word, at the self-confidence that precedes a fall, at truth that slips by drift, and at the minister's life and doctrine together.
webster_full: HEED, v.t. [Sax. hedan, to observe, to take care.] To mind; to regard with care; to take notice of; to attend to.
2. HEED, n. Care; attention; notice; observation; regard; often with take.
3. Caution; watchfulness against danger; as, to take heed of a snare.
4. Seriousness; a state of being earnest or attentive.
5. In Scripture, to take heed is often to beware, to guard the soul; take heed lest ye fall.
corruption_summary: Vigilance over the soul is recast as morbid introspection or anxiety, and the warnings against falling are muted by an assurance that never examines itself.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors both disable this word. The first hears every take heed as a threat to assurance and answers it with a slogan — once saved, always saved — used to silence the very warnings God gave for the preserving of his people. But Scripture's warnings are among the ordinary means by which the elect persevere; a man kept by God is kept partly by heeding. Perseverance of the saints is not the claim that a professing man cannot fall away, but that a truly regenerate man will not, and one reason he will not is that the Spirit makes such warnings land. The second error treats self-examination as unhealthy inwardness, and the modern vocabulary of anxiety is used to excuse a soul from ever looking at itself. 1 Corinthians 10:12 is addressed to exactly the man who would rather not.

The principle to recover is that heed has an external standard. Psalm 119:9 does not say a young man cleanses his way by being careful; it says by taking heed according to thy word. Introspection with no rule outside the self is a maze with no exit, and it deserves the modern suspicion it gets. Examination against Scripture is a different act entirely: it has a fixed measure, it can reach a verdict, and it ends in either repentance or peace rather than in endless circling.
roots_summary: Hebrew shamar is to keep, guard, watch over — the verb of keeping the garden and keeping the commandments. Greek blepo is to look at, and prosecho, to hold the mind toward.
roots_lines: Hebrew shamar (H8104) — to keep, guard, observe; used of Eden, of the law, and of the soul.
Hebrew nashab / qashab (H7181) — to prick up the ears, to attend closely to what is said.
Greek blepo (G991) — to see, to look to; take heed lest he fall, 1 Corinthians 10:12.
Greek prosecho (G4337) — to hold the mind toward, to give attention; Hebrews 2:1.
Greek epecho (G1907) — to hold fast, to give heed; take heed unto thyself, 1 Timothy 4:16.
usage: Of the cleansing of a young man's way: by taking heed thereto according to thy word (Psalm 119:9).
Of the peril of confidence: let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall (1 Corinthians 10:12).
Of truth lost by drift: lest at any time we should let them slip (Hebrews 2:1).
scriptures: Psalm 119:9

1 Corinthians 10:12

Hebrews 2:1
Therefore we ought to give the more earnest heed to the things which we have heard, lest at any time we should let them slip.
1 Timothy 4:16

pos: n. (extent from end to end; duration; rendering Hebrew orek, Greek mekos)
etymology: From the Saxon lengthu, from lang, long. Hebrew orek serves for both spatial extent and duration, so that length of days is as natural a phrase in that tongue as the length of a board.
biblical_def: Length in Scripture measures two things: space and life. Spatially it belongs to the tabernacle, the temple, and the city, where God gives exact dimensions and expects them kept — a fact that dignifies measurement itself and rebukes the notion that precision is unspiritual. Paul takes the vocabulary of measurement and applies it where it cannot finally be applied, praying that the saints “may be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height” (Ephesians 3:18) of the love of Christ — and then in the next breath calls that love a thing which passeth knowledge. The four dimensions are named precisely so that the reader will run out of them. Of life, length of days is a covenant blessing: Proverbs promises that wisdom brings “length of days, and long life, and peace” (Proverbs 3:2), and Moses tells Israel that the LORD “is thy life, and the length of thy days” (Deuteronomy 30:20) — the length is not an independent quantity but a Person's gift, and cleaving to him is the whole of the matter. The Psalter carries it past the grave: the king “asked life of thee, and thou gavest it him, even length of days for ever and ever” (Psalm 21:4), where the measure that began in a promise of long years on the land ends in the endless life of the Messiah and of those in him.
webster_summary: Extent from end to end; also duration. Scripture measures buildings exactly, measures life as a covenant gift, and names the four dimensions of Christ's love in order to show they will not contain it.
webster_full: LENGTH, n. [Sax. lengthu, from lang, long.] The extent of any thing material from end to end; the longest line which can be drawn through a body.
2. Extent of duration; as, the length of time, the length of a discourse.
3. Reach or expansion; extent; as, to run to a great length in argument.
4. Long continuance; as, the length of a disease.
5. At length, at full extent; also, at last, after a long time.
corruption_summary: Long life is treated as a bare medical achievement and the promise of length of days as an outdated bargain, while Ephesians 3:18 is read as though the love of Christ could be measured after all.
corruption_paragraphs: Where lifespan is regarded as a purely technical matter, the covenant framing of Deuteronomy 30:20 sounds primitive — as though obedience were a health regimen. But Moses is not offering a mechanism; he is naming a Person. He is thy life, and the length of thy days puts the years themselves in God's hand and makes cleaving to him the point rather than the price. The promise attached to the fifth commandment works the same way, and Paul repeats it to Christian children without embarrassment (Ephesians 6:2-3). Meanwhile the opposite error appears in devotional use of Ephesians 3:18, where the breadth and length and depth and height are treated as a set of measurements the diligent believer might eventually complete. Paul's own qualifier forbids it: the love he measures passeth knowledge. He piles up dimensions to exhaust them.

The principle to recover is that Scripture measures what God has measured and stops where he stops. The tabernacle has cubits because God gave cubits; the years of a life have a number because God numbers them; the love of Christ has four dimensions named and no total given. To insist on a number where God gave none is as much a failure of reverence as to despise the numbers he did give.
roots_summary: Hebrew orek covers extent and duration alike, so length of days is the natural idiom for long life. Greek mekos is spatial length; makrothumia, long-suffering, is length applied to patience.
roots_lines: Hebrew orek (H753) — length, of space or of days; from arak, to be long.
Hebrew arak (H748) — to prolong, to lengthen; that thy days may be long upon the land.
Greek mekos (G3372) — length; the dimension named in Ephesians 3:18 and Revelation 21:16.
Greek makros (G3117) — long, distant; of time and of space.
Greek makrothumia (G3115) — longsuffering, length of temper; patience measured as duration.
usage: Of the dimensions of Christ's love: the breadth, and length, and depth, and height (Ephesians 3:18).
Of long life as covenant gift: he is thy life, and the length of thy days (Deuteronomy 30:20).
Of life prolonged for ever: thou gavest it him, even length of days for ever and ever (Psalm 21:4).
